text.p: The $7 billion merger of Gillette Co and Duracell International Inc was met with a yawn in the debt markets on Friday, traders said.
"On the debt side it looks like this merger is a non-event," said one corporate bond desk manager. "At least for now."

The two companies announced the merger late Thursday. Gillette said it will issue about 108 million shares in the stock transaction, in which Duracell stockholders will receive 0.904 share of Gillette for each Duracell share owned.

Corporate traders qualified outstanding Gillette debt as "museum pieces" and rarely trades. According to Standard & Poor's Bond Guide for August, the firm has three outstanding note issues due in 1996, 2003 and 2005.
Gillette debt traditionally trades "very tight" to the market on the rare occasion, one trader said.
Duracell International's last long-term debt issue, $400 million 13.50 percent debt of 2000, was called in September of 1991, one source said.
Positive reception by two major ratings agencies failed to stir the interest of fixed-income market players.
Moody's Investors Service on Thursday affirmed Gillette's Aa3 senior unsecured debt rating and P-1 commercial paper rating. Moody's affirmed Duracell Inc's P-1 commercial paper.
Standard & Poor's said it may upgrade Gillette's AA-minus senior debt rating and Duracell's A-1 commercial paper rating. S&P affirmed Gillette's A1-plus commercial paper rating.
